# More results

These results use other methods than the one-arrow test on the
[main page](../README.md).

## Searching for the whole DAG

Hill climbing starts with no arrows. It adds, removes or reverses one arrow at a
time and keeps each change that raises the BIC. We ran it on 500 simulated farm
records, 100 times in each setting.

```{r search}
s <- imp[imp$n == 500, ]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(c("No other information", "Order of causes given",
               "5% of states recorded wrongly", "10% of states recorded wrongly"),
             round(19 * s$recall), round(100 * (1 - s$precision))),
  col.names = c("Setting", "Expert arrows found (of 19)",
                "Wrong arrows per 100 drawn"),
  align = "lrr", row.names = FALSE
)
```

An arrow counts as found only if it points the right way. "Order of causes given"
means the search was barred from drawing arrows backwards, for example from
`Livelihoods` to `TreeDiversity`. The order given was correct.

## Thirteen published studies

Each study was treated as one farm record, with a state chosen by hand for each
variable. Only `r lit$n_complete[1]` records were complete, and BIC needs complete
records. On those, a hill-climbing search drew
`r lit$arcs[lit$structure == "learned_from_scratch"]` arrows, more than the
expert's 19. A study is not a farm, and a sample this small cannot test the DAG.
